title: Celsus says the animals are nearer to God
source_text: Θέλων δ᾿ ἔτι διὰ πλειόνων μηδὲ τὰς περὶ τοῦ θείου ἐννοίας ἐξαιρέτους εἶναι παρὰ τὰ θνητὰ πάντα ἐν τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων τινὰ ἀποφῆναι ἐννοοῦντα περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ. περὶ οὗ τοιαῦται διαφωνίαι γεγόνασι καὶ τοῖς ὀξυτέροις τῶν πανταχοῦ ἀνθρώπων, Ἑλλήνων καὶ βαρβάρων, φησὶν ὅτι εἰ δ᾿, ὅτι θείας ἐννοίας ἄνθρωπος ἐπείληπται, νομίζεται ὑπερέχειν τῶν λοιπῶν ζῴων· ἴστωσαν οἱ τοῦτο φάσκοντες ὅτι καὶ τούτου πολλὰ τῶν ἄλλων ζῴων ἀντιποιηθήσεται· καὶ μάλ᾿ εἰκότως· τί γὰρ ἂν φαίη τις θειότερον τοῦ τὰ μέλλοντα προγινώσκειν τε καὶ προδηλοῦν; τοῦτο τοίνυν ἄνθρωποι παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων ζῴων καὶ μάλιστα παρ᾿ ὀρνίθων μανθάνουσιν· καὶ ὅσοι τῆς ἐκείνων ἐνδείξεως ἐπαΐουσιν, οὗτοι μαντικοί. εἰ δ᾿ ὄρνιθες ἄρα καὶ ὅσα (ἄλλα) ζῷα μαντικὰ ἐκ θεοῦ προγινώσκοντα διὰ συμβόλων ἡμᾶς διδάσκει, τοσοῦτον ἔοικεν ἐγγυτέρω τῆς θείας ὁμιλίας ἐκεῖνα πεφυκέναι καὶ εἶναι σοφώτερα καὶ θεοφιλέστερα. φασὶ δὲ τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ συνετοὶ καὶ ὁμιλίας ἐκείνοις εἶναι, δηλονότι τῶν ἡμετέρων ἱερωτέρας, καὶ αὐτοί που γνωρίζειν τὰ λεγόμενα καὶ ἔργῳ δεικνύειν ὅτι γνωρίζουσιν, ὅταν προειπόντες ὅτι ἔφασαν οἱ ὄρνιθες ὡς ἀπίασί ποι καὶ ποιήσουσι τόδε ἢ τόδε δεικνύωσιν ἀπελθόντας ἐκεῖ καὶ ποιοῦντας ἃ δὴ προεῖπον. ἐλεφάντων δὲ οὐδὲν εὐορκότερον οὐδὲ πρὸς τὰ θεῖα πιστότερον εἶναι δοκεῖ, πάντως δή που διότι γνῶσιν αὐτοῦ ἔχουσιν. ὅρα δὲ ἐν τούτοις, ὅσα ζητούμενα παρὰ τοῖς φιλοσοφοῦσιν οὐ μόνον Ἑλλήνων ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν ἐν βαρβάροις, εἴθ᾿ εὑρόντων εἴτε παρά τινων δαιμόνων μαθόντων τὰ περὶ οἰωνῶν καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ζῴων, ἀφ᾿ ὧν μαντεῖαί τινες ἀνθρώποις γίνεσθαι λέγονται, συναρπάζει καὶ ὡς ὁμολογούμενα ἐκτίθεται. πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ ἐζήτηται, πότερον ἔστι τις τέχνη οἰωνιστικὴ καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς ἡ διὰ ζῴων μαντικὴ ἢ οὐκ ἔστι· δεύτερον δὲ παρὰ τοῖς παραδεξαμένοις εἶναι τὴν δι᾿ ὀρνίθων μαντικὴν οὐ συμπεφώνηται ἡ αἰτία τοῦ τρόπου τῆς μαντείας· ἐπειδήπερ οἱ μὲν ἀπό τινων δαιμόνων ἢ θεῶν μαντικῶν φασι γίνεσθαι τὰς κινήσεις τοῖς ζῴοις, ὄρνισι μὲν εἰς διαφόρους πτήσεις καὶ εἰς διαφόρους φωνὰς τοῖς δὲ λοιποῖς εἰς τὰς τοιασδὶ κινήσεις ἢ τοιασδὶ, ἄλλοι δὲ θειοτέρας αὐτῶν καὶ πρὸς τοῦτ᾿ ἐπιτηδείους [αὐτῶν] εἶναι τὰς ψυχὰς, ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἀπιθανώτατον.
pass_a_gloss: Wishing still through more [words] [to show] that not even the notions (ἔννοιαι) about the divine (τὸ θεῖον) are special (ἐξαίρετοι) in the race of men beyond all mortal things, but to declare (ἀποφῆναι) some of the irrational animals also having notions about God (θεός), about whom such disagreements (διαφωνίαι) have arisen even for the sharper (ὀξύτεροι) of men everywhere, Greeks and barbarians, he says: CELSUS: 'If, because man has laid hold of (ἐπείληπται) divine notions, he is thought to excel (ὑπερέχειν) the remaining animals, let those asserting this know that many of the other animals also will lay claim (ἀντιποιηθήσεται) to this; and very reasonably (εἰκότως); for what would one say [is] more divine than to foreknow (προγινώσκειν) and foreshow (προδηλοῦν) the future? This then men learn from the other animals and most of all from birds (ὄρνιθες); and as many as understand (ἐπαΐουσιν) their indication (ἔνδειξις), these [are] diviners (μαντικοί). If then birds and as many [other] animals [are] prophetic (μαντικά), foreknowing from God (ἐκ θεοῦ), [and] teach us through signs (σύμβολα), by so much they seem to be by nature (πεφυκέναι) nearer to divine converse (θεία ὁμιλία) and to be wiser and more God-beloved (θεοφιλέστερα). And the intelligent (συνετοί) of men say there are also conversations (ὁμιλίαι) among them, clearly holier (ἱερώτεραι) than ours, and they themselves somewhere/somehow know the things said and show by deed that they know, when, having foretold that the birds said that they will go off somewhere and do this or that, they show [them] having gone there and doing what they foretold. Of elephants nothing seems more oath-keeping (εὐορκότερον) nor more faithful (πιστότερον) toward the divine things, surely because they have knowledge (γνῶσις) of it.' ORIGEN: See in these how many things inquired among those philosophizing, not only of Greeks but also of those among barbarians, whether having found or having learned from certain demons (δαίμονες) the things about omen-birds (οἰωνοί) and the other animals, from which certain divinations (μαντεῖαι) are said to come to men, he snatches up (συναρπάζει) and sets out as agreed (ὁμολογούμενα). For first it has been inquired whether there is some augural art (τέχνη οἰωνιστική) and simply the divination (μαντική) through animals or there is not; second, among those who accepted that the divination through birds exists, the cause (αἰτία) of the manner (τρόπος) of divination has not been agreed (συμπεφώνηται); since some say the movements (κινήσεις) come to be for the animals from certain demons or prophetic gods, for birds into different flights (πτήσεις) and different cries (φωναί), for the rest into such or such movements, but others [say] their souls (ψυχαί) are more divine and suited (ἐπιτήδειοι) for this, which is most unpersuasive (ἀπιθανώτατον).
pass_b_english: Wishing to show at still greater length that even notions about the divine are not the special mark of the human race above all mortal things, and to declare that some of the irrational animals too have notions about God, about whom such disagreements have arisen even among the sharpest of men everywhere, Greeks and barbarians alike, he says: “If man is thought to excel the other animals because he has grasped notions of the divine, let those who say so know that many of the other animals too will lay claim to this. And with very good reason. For what could one call more divine than to foreknow and foretell what is to come? This, then, men learn from the other animals, and above all from birds; and those who understand the signs they give are the diviners. If, then, birds and all the other prophetic animals, having foreknowledge from God, teach us through signs, they seem by so much to be nearer by nature to converse with the divine, and to be wiser and dearer to God. The men of understanding say that these creatures also have converse among themselves, plainly holier than ours, and that they themselves somehow understand what is said and show in deed that they understand: when they have foretold that the birds said they would go off somewhere and do this or that, they show them going there and doing just what they had foretold. And nothing seems to keep its oaths better than the elephant, or to be more loyal toward the divine, surely because elephants have knowledge of it.”

See in these words how many questions disputed among philosophers, not only among the Greeks but also among the barbarians, he snatches up and sets out as agreed. These philosophers either discovered, or learned from certain demons, what concerns omen-birds and the other animals from which, it is said, certain prophecies come to men. For first, it has been asked whether there is any art of augury, and in a word any divination through animals, or not. Second, among those who have accepted that divination through birds exists, there is no agreement on the cause of the manner of the divination. For some say that the animals are moved by certain demons or prophetic gods: birds to different flights and different cries, the others to this or that kind of movement. Others say that their souls are more divine and fitted for this, which is most unconvincing.

choices.choice: Opening: ἀποφῆναι depends on θέλων, so 'he declares that some ... have notions about God' (finite, asserted) became 'and to declare that some ... have notions about God' under 'Wishing'; the sentence now runs straight into 'he says:'
'Wishing still further, and at greater length' to 'Wishing to show at still greater length' (ἔτι διὰ πλειόνων, one idea)
ἐκ θεοῦ: 'foreknowing by God’s gift' to 'having foreknowledge from God' (removed added 'gift')
τῆς θείας ὁμιλίας: 'converse with God' to 'converse with the divine'
οἱ συνετοί: 'The wise among men' to 'The men of understanding' (keeps σοφός and συνετός apart)

Movement clause recast with the Greek agency: 'the animals are moved by certain demons or prophetic gods: birds to different flights ...' instead of 'movements are produced ... into', and ἐπειδήπερ kept as 'For'
Title 'Celsus Claims the Animals Know God Better' to 'Celsus Says the Animals Are Nearer to God' (matches ἐγγυτέρω τῆς θείας ὁμιλίας)

Celsus’s words are in double quotation marks, from “If man is thought” to “knowledge of it”; Origen’s reply begins at ὅρα δὲ ἐν τούτοις. Both infinitives in the opening (that notions of the divine are not special to man; ἀποφῆναι, to declare that some animals have notions of God) depend on θέλων, so both are kept under “Wishing”. ἐκ θεοῦ in Celsus’s mouth refers to the supreme God of his philosophy, so “God” is capitalised; θεῶν μαντικῶν (“prophetic gods”) are pagan gods, lower case. τῆς θείας ὁμιλίας rendered “converse with the divine” (not “with God”), as the Greek has the adjective. γνῶσιν αὐτοῦ: the antecedent is most naturally τὸ θεῖον implied in τὰ θεῖα, rendered “knowledge of it” (the divine); “of him” (God) is possible. οἱ συνετοί rendered “the men of understanding” to keep it apart from σοφός (“wise”) in the same passage. ὅσα (ἄλλα) ζῷα: Koetschau supplies ἄλλα; translated as supplied. ἐπιτηδείους [αὐτῶν]: Koetschau brackets the second αὐτῶν as intrusive; not translated. μαντικοί / μαντική rendered “diviners” / “divination”, ζῷα μαντικά “prophetic animals”; οἰωνοί “omen-birds”; τέχνη οἰωνιστική “art of augury”. δαίμονες rendered “demons”, Origen’s Christian sense. The genitive participles εἴθ᾿ εὑρόντων εἴτε … μαθόντων are taken with the philosophers (agreeing with Ἑλλήνων and τῶν ἐν βαρβάροις) and split into a separate sentence for readability. The elephant oath tradition is ancient natural-history lore; no source cited. No Scripture in this chapter.
